purpose: Rituximab-pvvr is used to treat certain types of blood cancers like non-Hodgkin's lymphoma and chronic lymphocytic leukemia. It is also used for autoimmune conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, and microscopic polyangiitis. It helps reduce symptoms and slow down the progression of these conditions.
how_it_works: Your immune system has certain white blood cells called B-cells, which can cause problems when there are too many of them or when they become cancerous. This medication works like a guided missile that finds and attaches to a specific target on those B-cells called CD20. Once attached, it signals your immune system to destroy those harmful cells, helping bring the disease under control.
common_side_effects: Infusion reactions such as fever, chills, nausea, headache, or rash during or shortly after the IV infusion are very common. You may also experience fatigue, low blood counts (which can increase infection risk), and stomach upset. Some patients notice muscle aches or a runny nose as well.
warnings: This medication can cause serious and sometimes life-threatening infusion reactions, so you will be closely monitored during each treatment. It can significantly lower your immune defenses, putting you at higher risk for serious infections including a rare but dangerous brain infection called PML. You should not receive live vaccines during treatment, and you must tell your doctor if you have a history of hepatitis B, as this drug can reactivate that virus. Always report any signs of infection like fever, chills, or unusual tiredness right away.
typical_dosing: This medication is given as an intravenous (IV) infusion directly into your vein, usually in a clinic or hospital setting. The dose and how often you receive it depends on what condition is being treated — for example, some patients receive it once a week for four weeks, while others may get it every few months. Your doctor will create a schedule that is right for your specific situation.
